text: An adherent is someone who has signed up to a set of beliefs and sticks to them — a follower of a doctrine, a movement or a party. The word is cooler and more formal than fan or member, and it points at the ideas a person holds rather than the club they joined, which is why it turns up so often in writing about religions and political philosophies. Here it marks out the people who genuinely believe in effective altruism, and the article's point is that for many of them the belief now cashes out as one mission: keeping AI from destroying humanity.

Empiricism, a position from philosophy that became the ground rule of modern science, says you settle a question by going and looking rather than by reasoning it out from first principles or taking an authority's word for it. An empiricist wants the measurement, the data, the experiment; the sibling adjective empirical means "based on observed evidence". The article credits effective altruists with it because the movement began by asking which donations measurably did the most good, not which causes felt worthiest.

Something grandiose is pitched far grander than it has any right to be: a plan, a claim or a style so sweeping and self-important that the scale itself is the problem. It is almost always an insult, and a precise one — it does not mean large, it means inflated, with a hint that the speaker is enjoying their own importance. Here it needles effective altruists who pair a spreadsheet with pronouncements about the fate of humanity.

Altruism means acting for someone else's good at a cost to yourself. Effective altruism — abbreviated EA, and its followers EAs — is the movement, started by philosophers at Oxford in the 2000s, that insists altruism should be judged by results rather than good intentions: work out where a dollar or an hour does the most measurable good, then send it there. The article's argument is that this harmless-sounding rule, followed strictly enough, leads somewhere very strange indeed.

A doctrine is a settled body of belief that a group teaches and expects its members to hold — originally religious, now used just as often of politics, law and the military, as in "military doctrine" or "legal doctrine". Calling effective altruism an ethical doctrine rather than an idea or a mood is deliberate: it signals a worked-out system with rules you can be held to.

To cook something up is to invent or concoct it, usually quickly and often with a hint that it was a bit made-up — you cook up an excuse, a scheme, a plan. Saying the doctrine was cooked up by philosophers in Oxford is mildly disrespectful on purpose: it makes a world-changing philosophy sound like something improvised in a kitchen.

The ivory tower is a standard put-down for university life: a place of beautiful ideas sealed off from ordinary practical reality. Someone in an ivory tower is clever but disconnected. The article uses it to measure a distance travelled — effective altruism went from the ivory tower to the corridors of power in about twenty years, which for a philosophy is startlingly fast.

The corridors of power means the places where real decisions get made — government ministries, the White House, the boardrooms of giant firms — and the image is of influence exercised quietly in hallways rather than in public. It became a set phrase after C.P. Snow's 1964 novel of that title.

Here staff is a verb, not a noun. To staff an organisation is to fill its jobs, to be the people working in it — so saying effective altruists "staff the world's leading artificial-intelligence companies" means they hold the posts inside those firms, not that they founded or own them. If you read staff as the familiar noun the sentence falls apart, which is why the verb is worth spotting.

The secretary of war is the civilian in the American cabinet who runs the armed forces and answers to the president. The job was called secretary of war until 1947, then secretary of defence for decades; the Trump administration brought the older, blunter title back. The Pentagon is the building the department works from, and the name is often used to mean the department itself.

To brand something is to stick a damning label on it so that the label sticks — the image is of burning a mark into an animal's hide. It is nearly always hostile: you brand a plan reckless, or a person a traitor. Here the secretary of war brands the philosophy "defective altruism", a pun that swaps effective for defective to suggest the whole thing is broken.

A utopia is an imagined perfect society; a dystopia is its opposite, an imagined society that has gone terribly wrong — the world of Nineteen Eighty-Four or The Hunger Games. Calling a real policy or philosophy dystopian accuses it of leading towards that kind of future, usually by way of control, surveillance or the sacrifice of individuals to a grand scheme.

Populism is a style of politics built on the claim that a pure, ordinary "people" is being betrayed by a corrupt elite, and that the leader speaks directly for them. It is not left or right by itself — there are populists of both kinds — and what marks it out is the us-against-the-elite framing. The article calls MAGA's version nostalgic populism because its promise points backwards, to restoring a lost past.

Short for "and company", borrowed from old business names. Tacked onto a person or movement — "MAGA and Co" — it means that group and its various allies and hangers-on, lumped together without bothering to name them. It is casual and faintly dismissive.

Here subjects is a verb, stressed on the second syllable (sub-JECTS), and to subject something to a process is to force it to undergo that process. A patient is subjected to tests; a metal is subjected to heat. So a movement that "subjects the world to complex moral calculations" is putting the whole world through its arithmetic whether the world asked for it or not — a very different word from the school subject or the subject of a sentence.

A mint is the factory where a government stamps out coins, so to mint is literally to manufacture money. Journalists stretch it to mean creating new rich people at speed: a boom mints millionaires. Saying the technology "mints more billionaires" compresses the whole process — company founded, shares sold, fortune made — into one word.

A channel is a cut groove that water has to follow, and as a verb to channel money is to direct it down a chosen path rather than letting it spread wherever. Nothing to do with television channels. Effective altruists who "channel billions of dollars to causes" are deciding which few causes the money reaches.

This is not cause-and-effect. A cause in this sense is a goal people organise and give money to because they believe in it — ending malaria, saving a forest, animal welfare. The phrase "a good cause" is the everyday version. Watching which causes get the money is how you tell what a movement actually believes, which is exactly what the article is doing.

OpenAI is the American company that built ChatGPT, founded in 2015 and now one of the two or three most important AI firms in the world. It was started partly by people worried that AI would be developed carelessly, the idea being that it was safer to build it themselves — which is the irony the article points at.

Anthropic is the American AI company behind the Claude models, founded in 2021 by people who had left OpenAI. It markets itself on safety and has been the most willing of the big labs to refuse certain uses of its models — including, as the article notes, some military ones, which is what the Trump administration has feuded with it over.

In writing about AI, a lab means a whole company — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind — not a room with benches and beakers. The word stuck because these firms began as research outfits, and it flatters them a little by making multibillion-dollar businesses sound like scientific institutes. Read "the leading labs" as "the leading AI companies".

To throttle someone is to choke them by the throat; to throttle a machine is to cut the fuel reaching it. Both senses feed the figurative one: throttling an industry means restricting it until it slows down or stops. The Trump administration's fear is that effective altruists will succeed in slowing AI deliberately.

A firm is simply a company — standard usage in business journalism, and nothing to do with firm meaning solid or strict. It is most at home with professional partnerships (a law firm, an accounting firm) but gets applied to any business. "The firm's refusal" here means Anthropic's refusal.

In AI, a model is one trained system — the thing you actually talk to, like GPT-5 or Claude. The name comes from statistics, where a model is a mathematical description of some pattern in data, and that is literally what it is: a very large set of numbers, adjusted during training until the system reproduces patterns found in its training data. Nothing to do with fashion models or scale models, and companies release numbered versions of them the way phone makers release handsets.

Benign means harmless, even kindly — a benign ruler, a benign climate — and in medicine a benign tumour is one that will not spread, as opposed to a malignant one. Saying AI may prove "hugely benign" concedes that it could turn out wonderfully. That concession matters to the article's argument: the leading effective altruists are not people who think AI is bound to be bad, only that it might be, which is a much harder position to dismiss.

To run amok is to go on an uncontrolled rampage. The word came into English from Malay in the 1600s and has kept its sense of violence that cannot be reasoned with — a crowd runs amok, a bull runs amok. Used of a machine-brain, it pictures a system pursuing its goal with total force and no judgement, which is precisely the risk effective altruists worry about.

In pursuit of means chasing after, with the suggestion of single-mindedness — in pursuit of profit, in pursuit of the truth. The article uses it twice, once for a machine chasing goals that are misaligned with ours and once, approvingly, for EAs who will debate any topic in pursuit of the truth. The same determination looks admirable in people and alarming in software.

Alignment is the term of art in AI research for getting a system's goals to match what humans actually want; a misaligned system is one whose goals have come apart from ours. The worry is not that a machine turns evil but that it pursues the objective it was given with such thoroughness that it tramples everything you forgot to mention. The article puts it in quotation marks because it is EA jargon that has since become the standard word.

A doomer is someone convinced that catastrophe is coming, and AI doomerism is the belief that advanced AI is likely to destroy humanity. It started as an insult and was partly adopted by the people it was aimed at. Note that the article is describing critics attacking doomerism, not endorsing the label.

t: play the nerd than the ball
forms: play the nerd than the ball
text: This twists a well-known sporting phrase: "play the ball, not the man" means tackle the argument rather than the person making it, and a player who does the opposite is fouling. Saying critics find it easier to play the nerd than the ball accuses them of mocking effective altruists as weirdos instead of answering what they actually claim. Whenever you meet the phrase in a debate, it is a charge of changing the subject to the opponent.

Crude means rough and unrefined, and when applied to an argument it means too simple to be fair — missing the distinctions that matter. Not rude, and not crude oil. The article uses it in both directions: the critics' attack on EA is "too crude", while EAs' own reasoning about extinction rests on a "crude moral arithmetic". Each side is accused of flattening something complicated.

Esteem is the respect in which something is held, and the standard phrase is to hold something in high esteem. Holding reason in higher esteem than tradition or norms means ranking a good argument above an inherited custom whenever the two collide. The related self-esteem is the respect you hold yourself in.

In philosophy a rationalist trusts reasoning over sense experience — the opposite pole from an empiricist. But the quotation marks here point at something newer: the online rationalist community, a set of blogs and forums from the late 2000s devoted to thinking clearly and avoiding mental biases. It overlapped so heavily with effective altruism that the two largely merged, which is the blending the article mentions.

Norms are the unwritten rules a group actually lives by — what counts as polite, what everyone does without being told, what gets you frowned at. The word is standard in sociology and politics, where "democratic norms" means the habits that keep a system working even where no law requires them. The point of pairing norms with tradition is that both are inherited rather than argued for, which is exactly why EAs rank them below reason.

Utilitarianism is the moral theory, worked out by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill in the 1800s, that the right act is whichever produces the greatest total wellbeing — "the greatest good for the greatest number". Its signature move is to treat a moral question as a sum to be maximised, counting everyone's happiness equally and nobody's twice. Effective altruism is its most energetic modern descendant, which is why the article says EAs reduce ethics to an optimisation problem.

Boiling a liquid down drives off the water and leaves the concentrated essence, so to boil something down to X is to strip it to its core. The phrase splits around its object — you boil a long argument down to one claim. Saying EAs boil ethical behaviour down to an optimisation problem is a criticism as much as a description: something is being left in the pot.

To optimise is to find the setting that makes some quantity as large or as small as possible — the fastest route, the cheapest design, the highest score. An optimisation problem is a question posed in that shape: here is the thing to maximise, here are the constraints, now find the best answer. The article's complaint is about what happens when morality is posed that way, because an optimiser pushes all the way to the extreme and takes any shortcut the rules allow. (Optimisation is the British spelling; Americans write optimization.)

Not the branch of mathematics you meet in school. In this older and broader sense a calculus is any systematic way of reckoning something up — the considerations you weigh and how you trade them off, as in "the political calculus" or "a moral calculus". Saying that EAs' calculus downplays local duties means their whole method of weighing gives little weight to keeping promises or looking after your own family.

An imperative is something you simply must do — an obligation that does not wait on whether you feel like it. In grammar the imperative is the commanding form of a verb ("Go!"), and the moral sense keeps that force. The local imperatives the article lists are small, binding duties to the people right around you: keep promises, look after your family.

To be impartial is to take no side and play no favourites — what we demand of a referee or a judge. Impartiality is normally a virtue, so there is a real jolt in applying it here: reducing suffering impartially means a stranger's pain counts exactly as much as your own child's. That is the step most people will not take, and the article is showing you that EAs take it deliberately rather than by accident.

To factor something in is to include it in a calculation so that it affects the answer — you factor in traffic when working out when to leave. The word comes from arithmetic, where factors are the numbers multiplied together. Effective altruists who factor a very wide circle of concerns into their moral calculations are letting far more beings into the sum than most people do.

Consulting is the industry of being hired to advise other companies — a firm brings in consultants to analyse a problem, recommend a strategy and leave. Along with banking it is one of the standard high-paying destinations for ambitious graduates, which is why it appears here: early effective altruism told its recruits to take those jobs on purpose and give the money away, rather than becoming charity workers themselves.

Good works means acts of charity and service — feeding the hungry, caring for the sick. The phrase comes from Christian theology, where it named the deeds by which faith shows itself, and it keeps a faintly old-fashioned, moral ring. Saying wealth "could buy good works" is pointed: it turns virtue into something purchasable, which is the whole logic being examined.

Your intuition is what feels obviously right before you have reasoned about it. Something counterintuitive runs against that feeling while still, perhaps, being true — that a heavy object and a light one fall at the same rate is counterintuitive. The article uses the word three times, and the shift is the point: EAs treat a counterintuitive conclusion as a sign they are thinking well, while the article argues it can be a warning that a step in the argument went wrong.

A balance is a pair of scales, so to weigh something in the balance is to put it on the scales and let it count in the verdict. The phrase is biblical and carries a sense of final judgement. Saying those not yet born "should be weighed in the balance" means people who do not exist yet are placed on the scales alongside the living.

Longtermism is the position, developed inside effective altruism, that because the future could contain vastly more people than the present, protecting that future matters more than almost anything happening now. A longtermist therefore works on risks that could end or permanently damage humanity rather than on present-day suffering. The article's objection is in its last clause: that priority can starve today's good causes.

To forestall something is to act in advance to stop it happening — you forestall an objection by answering it before it is raised. It is a useful word because it names prevention done early, before the problem is visible. Longtermists who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future are trying to head off disasters that have not begun.

Beyond the literal sense, to starve something is to deprive it of what it needs to keep going — a starved budget, a department starved of staff. Saying longtermism "starves today's good causes" means money and effort are pulled away until those causes wither. The word is doing deliberate double duty, because some of the causes being starved are themselves about feeding people.

Factory farming is raising animals for food at industrial scale and density — tens of thousands of chickens or pigs indoors, bred and fed for maximum output. It makes meat cheap, and critics argue it imposes enormous suffering on a vast number of animals. That arithmetic of scale is why it became a major effective-altruist cause.

This is not a joke, and it follows directly from EA's method. Hundreds of billions of shrimp are farmed each year, far more than any farmed mammal, so if shrimp can suffer even slightly then the total suffering is astronomical — and because almost nobody works on it, a dollar spent there buys an unusually large reduction in suffering. Shrimp welfare has become a real, funded effective-altruist cause, and the article offers it as an example of where the logic ends up.

Repugnant means so offensive that it provokes disgust — a reaction in the gut, not just disagreement. It is the strongest word in this part of the article, and the distinction it draws is deliberate: a counterintuitive conclusion merely surprises you, while a repugnant one is the kind that most people think no argument could ever make acceptable.

In aggregate means added all together, as one total, rather than taken one at a time. It is the standard phrase for switching from the individual to the sum, and the switch can change an answer completely: one insect counts for almost nothing, but insects in aggregate are so numerous that some EAs conclude their lives outweigh all human life. Spotting the move from "each" to "in aggregate" is often the key to an argument like this.

Welfare here means wellbeing — whether a creature's life is going well or badly — as in animal welfare or child welfare. In America the word is also shorthand for government payments to the poor, but that is not the sense in use. The article asks it of an unusual subject: some EAs believe the welfare of AI systems themselves will one day matter.

Read aloud as "p of doom", this is AI-world slang for the probability that artificial intelligence causes human extinction. The p is the standard mathematical notation for probability. People in the field genuinely quote a personal number — one per cent, ten per cent — and the subheading jokes that EA plus AI equals exactly this question.

To revere something is to hold it in deep, almost religious respect. The noun is reverence, and a revered figure is one treated as beyond criticism. The sentence "It is right to revere reason" is doing careful work: the article is granting that respect for reason is correct, and only then arguing that reverence can be pushed too far.

John Rawls (1921–2002) was the most influential political philosopher of the twentieth century, best known for asking what rules you would choose for a society if you did not yet know who in it you would be. Pairing him with Aristotle spans more than two thousand years of moral philosophy, which is the point: the article is claiming that thinkers across that whole range agreed an argument leading somewhere intolerable must contain a hidden mistake.

A perverse conclusion is one that is twisted away from what is sensible or right — turned backwards, as though wrongness were the point. The related economic phrase "perverse incentive" names a reward that produces the opposite of what was intended. The article's charge is that EAs enjoy perverse conclusions, treating the discomfort as evidence of clear thinking.

A margin of error is the honest admission of how wrong a number might be — the "plus or minus three points" attached to an opinion poll. It is central to statistics because a result without one pretends to a precision it does not have. The article's objection is that effective-altruist calculations carry margins of error so enormous that the answers they produce cannot bear any weight.

A quandary is a situation in which you genuinely do not know what to do because the options are all unattractive — a dilemma, with the emphasis on being stuck. Moral quandaries involving billions of people are the hardest kind, and the article's claim is blunt: nobody is truly capable of weighing them.

A discount rate is the number economists use to convert future value into present value — how much less a benefit is worth to us because it arrives later rather than now. It is why a dollar next year is worth slightly less than a dollar today, and it is the most argued-over number in climate policy, because a small change in it transforms how much the fate of people in 2200 should cost us today. The article lists it among the quantities EAs must guess at.

Dire means dreadful in the fullest sense — a dire warning, dire poverty, dire consequences. It is a strong word and should be kept for genuinely grave things, which is why it fits extinction. Note that the word is being used to carry an argument: because extinction is so dire, even a tiny chance of it comes out large once it is multiplied.

Flesh-and-blood means real, living and physically present, as opposed to theoretical or imagined — a flesh-and-blood person rather than a character or a statistic. The contrast is the heart of the sentence: on one side today's flesh-and-blood concerns, actual people suffering now, and on the other a calculated risk to people who may never exist.

Something inherent belongs to a thing in itself and cannot be taken away or granted by anyone else — an inherent flaw, an inherent right. Saying each person has inherent dignity means the worth is simply there, not earned and not dependent on how useful the person is. That claim is the main rival to the view that people's value is something to be added up.

To anoint someone is to pour oil on them, the ancient ritual by which kings and priests were marked out as chosen. The modern figurative sense is to designate someone as the chosen one — a retiring boss anoints a successor. The sting in "anointing themself" is the self: the oil is being poured by the same hand that is claiming the authority.

Central planning is running an economy from the centre by decision rather than by prices — officials decide how much steel to make and where it goes, instead of leaving it to buyers and sellers. The Soviet Union was the great attempt, and it is remembered for shortages and for overruling what people actually wanted. Calling an effective altruist one step from being a central planner is a precise accusation: someone with a spreadsheet, total confidence and the power to decide on everyone's behalf.

The French revolution began in 1789, overthrew the monarchy, and declared a new order founded on reason and the rights of man. Within a few years it had turned into the Terror, executing thousands — including nuns — by guillotine, the machine built to behead people quickly and efficiently. It is the standard historical example of a movement built on reason that ended in mass killing, which is exactly why the article reaches for it.

Vladimir Lenin led the 1917 Russian revolution and founded the Soviet Union. He argued that a small group of revolutionaries who had properly understood the theory should rule on the workers' behalf — the specific habit of mind the article is pointing at, where mastering the argument becomes a licence to act for people without asking them.

Marxism is the body of theory from Karl Marx holding that history is driven by conflict between economic classes and that capitalism will be replaced by workers' ownership. What matters to the article is its claim to be scientific: because Marxism presented itself as having worked out where history was going, intellectuals who had mastered it could believe they knew workers' real interests better than the workers did.

Let alone introduces something even more extreme than what you just said, to show how far the claim stretches — "he cannot drive a car, let alone a lorry". It only works downhill from the harder case. "Billions today, let alone trillions of future ones" says that if the first calculation is already beyond us, the second is hopeless.

To fall into a trap is to make a mistake that was lying in wait for you, usually one others have made before. The closing sentence turns the article's own argument around: effective altruists warn that a machine might lock onto a single wrong objective, and the final worry is that a small group of people, doing exactly that, would fall into the same trap.
